summary: Presents objectives for an interoperable protocol for the Control and Provisioning of Wireless Access Points. It aims to set focused requirements for developing and evaluating such a protocol, covering architecture, operation, security and network operator needs. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4564 is a list of requirements for a protocol that would let a central controller configure and manage wireless access points made by different manufacturers. It says what such a protocol must and should do, and it deliberately does not define the protocol itself.

questions: what is a wireless termination point
subtitle: The wish list for a protocol that lets one controller configure and manage many wireless access points, whatever their design.

tldr.problem: A large wireless network has hundreds or thousands of access points, and each vendor solved the control and configuration problem differently, so equipment from different suppliers cannot be run together.
tldr.mechanism: The document lists the objectives such a protocol must meet, split into architecture, operations and security, and each objective is marked mandatory, desirable or a non-objective, with the mandatory ones written as requirements a protocol MUST satisfy.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational document that defines no protocol. It was written to be used with the CAPWAP problem statement and architecture taxonomy to design and evaluate one.

today: RFC 4564 is an Informational document from July 2006 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It states objectives for a CAPWAP protocol rather than the protocol itself, and it was written to be used with the CAPWAP problem statement, RFC 3990, and the architecture taxonomy, RFC 4118, to develop and evaluate an interoperable protocol.

sections.title: What CAPWAP Is For
sections.content:
The growth of large-scale wireless LAN deployments has brought a number of technical challenges into focus. One is the complexity of managing large numbers of Wireless Termination Points, which is made worse by variations in their design. Another is maintaining consistent configurations among the many termination points of a system. The dynamic nature of the wireless medium is also a concern, together with wireless LAN security. These challenges have been highlighted in RFC 3990.

Many vendors addressed the challenges with their own architectures, and a survey of those developments was conducted to understand the context better. The result was the Architecture Taxonomy, RFC 4118, which classifies the major wireless LAN architecture families. Broadly, these are the autonomous, the centralized wireless LAN, and the distributed mesh architectures.

The Taxonomy identified the centralized architecture as one in which portions of the wireless medium access control operations are centralised in a wireless LAN controller. That architecture is further classified into remote-MAC, split-MAC and local-MAC designs, each differing in the degree of separation of the wireless MAC layer capabilities between the termination points and the controller.

The CAPWAP framework covers the local-MAC and split-MAC designs, and that is where standardisation effort is focused. The CAPWAP protocol is the protocol between the wireless LAN controller and the termination points, and it facilitates the control, management and provisioning of those points in an interoperable manner. The document puts forward critical objectives for achieving interoperability in that framework, so that equipment of the major design types can be deployed and managed together.
sections.plainLanguage: Wireless networks have controllers that manage the access points, and every manufacturer built that part differently. CAPWAP is the attempt to define one protocol that works across the two most common controller designs, so equipment from different suppliers can be run together.

sections.title: How the Objectives Are Prioritised
sections.content:
The objectives are classified by the aspect they address. Architecture objectives deal with system-level aspects of the protocol: protocol extensibility, diversity in network deployments and architecture designs, and differences in transport technologies. Operational objectives deal with the control and management features, covering monitoring, resource management, quality of service and access control. Security objectives address threats to the wireless LANs and their containment, covering both the protocol between the controller and the termination points and the wireless LAN system as a whole.

On top of that classification, each objective is given a priority. The mandatory and accepted objectives have been deemed crucial for the control and provisioning of termination points, they address the challenges of large-scale deployments directly, and a CAPWAP protocol must realise them. The desirable objectives would help improve control of wireless LANs but need not be required for all networks or scenarios. The non-objectives were prioritised as such during working group consultations, though they may be applicable in other contexts.

A separate category covers requirements gathered from network service operators, which are specific needs arising from operators' experience of deploying and managing large-scale wireless LANs. The document uses the RFC 2119 requirement keywords throughout, so an objective stated as a MUST is a requirement on any protocol that claims to be CAPWAP.
sections.plainLanguage: Every objective is marked with how important it is. The mandatory ones are requirements the protocol has to meet, the desirable ones are worth having, and the non-objectives are things CAPWAP deliberately leaves alone.

sections.title: Logical Groups and Traffic Separation
sections.content:
A logical group is a logical separation of a physical termination point, so a single physical device operates a number of logical groups. Virtual access points are examples of logical groups, and each Basic Service Set Identifier and the radios of the constituent wireless terminals are denoted as distinct logical groups of a physical termination point.

Shared wireless LAN deployments, where a single physical infrastructure supports a number of logical networks, are increasingly used because they let deployment and management costs be spread across businesses. In traditional wireless LANs each physical termination point represents one complete subset of a larger system. In shared deployments each physical termination point represents a number of logical subsets of possibly a number of larger systems, and the wireless LANs are managed in terms of logical groups rather than physical devices. The protocol must therefore be capable of controlling and managing physical termination points in terms of logical groups, including those based on Basic Service Set Identifiers, and must provide provisions for configuring logical groups at the device in all operating modes, whether the device bridges locally or the controller bridges centrally.

The second architecture requirement is traffic separation. The centralised architecture consolidates portions of the wireless MAC functionality at a central controller and distributes the rest across the termination points, so the two exchange control and data information. The objective is that the control and data aspects be mutually separated, which allows each type of exchange to be optimised independently. The protocol must define transport control messages so that the transport of control messages is separate from the transport of data messages. In the context of shared deployments, the separation of control and data also addresses security: where different logical groups, such as those established by different virtual access points, are managed by different administrators, separation is a first step towards containing and securing each group. Traffic from each logical group must also be mutually separated to keep the groups independent.
sections.plainLanguage: One physical access point can act as several virtual ones, each serving a different customer, and the protocol has to manage it that way. The messages that control the network and the messages that carry the traffic have to travel on separate paths, so that one customer cannot interfere with another.

sections.title: Configuration Consistency, Monitoring and Quality of Service
sections.content:
A wireless LAN in the CAPWAP framework contains many termination points, each needing to be configured and managed in a consistent manner. The main concern is the availability of information about their configuration states, which can be achieved by giving the controller regular updates on the state of their operations. The protocol must include support for regular exchanges of state information between the termination points and the controller, with examples of that state including processing load and memory utilisation.

One aspect of configuration consistency is the firmware. The scale of large wireless LANs introduces the possibility of variations in the firmware used among the devices, so the protocol must support a trigger for delivering firmware updates, though the actual delivery of the firmware need not be part of the protocol.

The protocol must also allow for the exchange of statistics, congestion and other state information. In the switching segment, network congestion, device status and firmware information have to be monitored; in the wireless medium segment, the dynamic nature of the medium itself has to be monitored. The protocol should be able to monitor these sources and deliver the results to the relevant devices, and should combine state information from them, for example merging statistics and status signals before exchanging them. Examples of the statistics to monitor include congestion state, interference levels, loss rates and various delay factors.

Quality of service has to be coordinated across both segments, since performance and quality are what a wireless network offers its subscribers. Because the two segments are fundamentally different, alternate quality of service mechanisms are likely between the termination points and the subscribers, based on IEEE 802.11e, and between the termination points and the controllers. Resources therefore need to be adjusted in a coordinated fashion over both segments, and the protocol must ensure those adjustments are exchanged between controllers and termination points. The protocol must map the IEEE 802.11e quality of service priorities to equivalent priorities across the switching and wireless medium segments, and should not be restricted to 802.11e-based mapping, since other 802.11 task groups including TGk, TGu and TGv may also affect network resources.
sections.plainLanguage: The controller has to know what the access points are doing, so that it can keep them configured the same way and give them the same settings for priority traffic. The protocol has to carry those status reports, trigger firmware updates, and translate the wireless priority scheme into the one used on the wired side.

sections.title: Security Requirements
sections.content:
The protocol must first let the participating entities, the wireless LAN controller and the termination points, authenticate each other explicitly. This is to ensure that rogue elements do not gain access to the wireless LAN system: rogue termination points should not breach legitimate wireless LANs, and rogue controllers should not gain control of legitimate termination points. The termination points may need to renew their authentication state with the controller regularly, and the same for controllers.

If authentication is performed through an authenticated key exchange, future knowledge of the derived keys must not be sufficient for authentication. Any session keys used between the controller and the termination points must be mutually derived using entropy contributed by both parties, so that no one party controls the resulting session keys.

Once the two sides are mutually authenticated, the information exchanged between them must be secured. The protocol must provide integrity protection and replay protection, and should provide confidentiality through encryption, covering illegitimate modification of exchanges, eavesdropping and denial of service attacks. The key establishment protocol must also be designed to minimise the possibility of future compromises after the keys are established. The protocol must not prevent the use of asymmetric authentication, and if it meets the criteria that require automated key management per BCP 107, mutual authentication must be accomplished through an authenticated key exchange.

System-wide security is about threats outside the centralised segment, in particular rogue wireless clients and other illegitimate wireless interference. One aspect is the sharing of the Pairwise Master Key across termination points, which raises the ambiguity between legitimate sharing and illegitimate copies, and the design must not allow external entities to compromise the wireless LAN system. The security considerations section adds that the framework highlights support for both local-MAC and split-MAC designs, and that in a shared deployment the traffic of each logical group needs to be mutually separated, so that data or control traffic from one group cannot stray into or influence another. It also notes that the low cost of launching attacks makes the protocol a target, that profiles for denial of service and replay attacks need to be considered, that the open environment of many deployments makes physical security breaches highly probable and that compromises from theft and physical damage must be considered, so that a single compromised termination point cannot affect the wireless LAN as a whole. Finally, it observes that asymmetric, non-mutual authentication between termination points and the controller carries a risk that a rogue participant exploits, that it is preferable to avoid it, and that it may be acceptable where the legitimacy of the participants is verified externally, for example by physical containment within a close environment.
sections.plainLanguage: The controller and the access points have to prove who they are to each other before anything else happens, and the keys they use have to depend on both of them. Access points and controllers also have to be protected from each other, and no single compromised access point should be able to damage the whole network.

sections.title: Interoperability Between Local-MAC and Split-MAC
sections.content:
The two major designs of the centralised architecture are local-MAC and split-MAC, and with standardisation focused on both it is crucial that they interoperate. The objective is that termination points of both designs can work together within a single wireless LAN, so that one controller can control both types over a single CAPWAP protocol.

The designs differ in the degree of 802.11 MAC functionality each type of termination point realises, and the major distinction between them is how 802.11 MAC frames are processed. The protocol should therefore include functionality allowing negotiation of significant capabilities between the termination points and the controller, and as a first step such negotiation could cover the type of the termination point, split-MAC or local-MAC, because that gives substantial information about its capabilities. The capability differences among different termination points equate to alternative interfaces with the controller, so the protocol should adapt its operations to the major different interfaces, with the finer granularity of functionality based on the access point functionality documents produced by the IEEE 802.11 AP Functionality Ad-Hoc Committee. The protocol must include sufficient capability negotiation to distinguish between the major types of termination point.

Other objectives cover the remaining architectural ground. Wireless terminals must not be required to recognise or be aware of the CAPWAP protocol, which keeps the setup cost down because the many existing terminals need not be altered. Any vendor or person must be able to implement the protocol from the specification alone, and those implementations must interoperate. A termination point vendor should be able to modify its hardware without any controller vendor involvement, and the protocol must not limit vendors in their choice of local-MAC or split-MAC. It must not prevent the operation of established methods of NAT traversal, and it must not be constrained to specific underlying transport mechanisms, so it can run over IPv4 and IPv6 and inside tightly administered networks or on open public access networks. The desirable objectives add support for authentication mechanisms other than IEEE 802.11i, support for future wireless technologies such as IEEE 802.16, and openness to new IEEE 802.11 definitions and extensions.
sections.plainLanguage: The same controller has to be able to run access points that keep their radio functions locally and access points that split them with the controller. To do that the controller and the access point negotiate what each can do, and the protocol adapts accordingly.
